source_refs.note: Book p. 38-40: formulas (i)-(vi), Proof (1) sin^-1, Proof (2) cot^-1, Proof (3) sec^-1, Challenge! and Recall! boxes, Example 6

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why these need care: an inverse trigonometric function such as \(\sin^{-1} x\) is the angle whose sine is \(x\). Each one is defined on a principal range (so that it is a function, with one output for each input). Every proof below uses that range to decide the sign of a square root.
Pattern: the three co-functions (ii), (iv), (vi) are the negatives of (i), (iii), (v).

blocks.caption: Domains and principal ranges used in the proofs (our table)

blocks.text: Proof (1)

Let \(y = \sin^{-1}(x)\), where \(x \in [-1, 1]\) and \(y \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).
\[\sin y = x \quad \ldots(1)\]
Differentiate equation (1) w.r.t. \(x\), we have
\[\cos y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1\]
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{\cos y} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\cos^{2} y}}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^{2} y}}\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin^{-1} x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\]
for \(x \in (-1, 1)\) \((\because \sin y = x)\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The method in every proof: write the inverse function as an ordinary trigonometric equation, differentiate implicitly (2.3.3), and change the answer back into \(x\).
Why \(\cos y = +\sqrt{1 - \sin^{2} y}\): for \(y \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) the cosine is never negative, so the positive square root is the right one.
Why \(x \ne \pm 1\): there \(\cos y = 0\) and we cannot divide by it; the graph of \(\sin^{-1} x\) has vertical tangents at its two ends.
Proof (2)

Let \(y = \cot^{-1}(x)\), where \(y \in (0, \pi)\) and \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[\cot y = x \quad \ldots(2)\]
We differentiate equation (1) w.r.t. \(x\),
\[-\csc^{2} y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1\]
\(\left((\cot y)' = -\csc^{2} y\right)\)
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{1}{\csc^{2} y}\]
\((\csc y \ne 0, \text{ for } y \in (0, \pi))\)
\[= -\dfrac{1}{1 + \cot^{2} y}\]
\((\because 1 + \cot^{2} y = \csc^{2} y)\)
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cot^{-1} x) = -\dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\]
for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) \((\because \cot y = x)\)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Proof (2) the equation \(\cot y = x\) is labelled (2), but the next line says 'We differentiate equation (1)'. It should say 'We differentiate equation (2)' (the equation \(\cot y = x\)).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book numbers its proofs 1, 2, 3, but the formulas are numbered (i) to (vi). Proof (2) proves formula (iv), \(\cot^{-1} x\), and Proof (3) proves formula (v), \(\sec^{-1} x\).
Here no sign problem arises: \(\csc^{2} y = 1 + \cot^{2} y\) holds without any square root, so the formula is valid for every real \(x\).
Proof (3)

Let \(y = \sec^{-1} x\), where \(x \in (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\) and \(y \in [0, \pi] - \left\{\frac{\pi}{2}\right\}\)
\[\sec y = x \quad \ldots(1), \quad |x| \ge 1\]
We differentiate equation (1) w.r.t. \(x\):
\[\sec y\tan y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1\]
\(\left(\because (\sec y)' = \sec y\tan y\right)\)
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{\sec y\tan y}\]
where \(\sec y \ne 0\) and \(\tan y \ne 0\)
\(\tan y \ne 0 \Rightarrow y \ne 0\) and \(y \ne \pi \Rightarrow x \ne -1, 1\) and from equation (1).
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{x\tan y} \quad \ldots(2)\]
\((\because \sec y = x)\)
\[\tan y = \begin{cases}\sqrt{\tan^{2} y}, & y \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ -\sqrt{\tan^{2} y}, & y \in \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)\end{cases}\]
\[= \begin{cases}\sqrt{\sec^{2} y - 1}, & y \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ -\sqrt{\sec^{2} y - 1}, & y \in \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)\end{cases}\]
\[\tan y = \begin{cases}\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}, & x \in (1, \infty) \\ -\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}, & x \in (-\infty, -1)\end{cases}\]

\[\tan y = \begin{cases}\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}, & x \in (1, -1) \\ -\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}, & x \in (-\infty, 1)\end{cases}\]
\(\left(\because \sec y = x,\ \text{and } x \in (1, \infty) \text{ when } y \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right),\right.\) \(\left.\text{while } x \in (-\infty, -1) \text{ when } y \in \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)\right)\)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
After writing \(\tan y\) correctly, the book repeats it with wrong intervals: \(x \in (1, -1)\) and \(x \in (-\infty, 1)\). The correct intervals (as in the line just before, and as the book's own reason says) are:
\[\tan y = \begin{cases}\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}, & x \in (1, \infty) \\ -\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}, & x \in (-\infty, -1)\end{cases}\]

Substitute the value of \(\tan y\) in equation (2)
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{x\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}}, & x \in (1, \infty) \\[2mm] \dfrac{1}{-x\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}}, & x \in (-\infty, -1)\end{cases}\]
Hence,
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec^{-1} x) = \dfrac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}}\]
where \(x \in (-\infty, -1) \cup (1, \infty)\) \(\left(\because |x| = \begin{cases}x & \text{if } x \ge 0 \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0\end{cases}\right)\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why two cases: \(\tan y = \pm\sqrt{\sec^{2} y - 1}\) and the sign depends on the quadrant. For \(y \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), \(x = \sec y > 1\) and \(\tan y > 0\); for \(y \in \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)\), \(x = \sec y < -1\) and \(\tan y < 0\).
In both cases \(x\tan y\) is positive and equals \(|x|\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}\): when \(x > 1\) it is \(x\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}\), and when \(x < -1\) it is \((-x)\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}\). That is why \(|x|\) appears.

blocks.title: Challenge!
blocks.text: Prove formulae (2), (3) and (5).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Formula (5), that is (v), is already proved above as Proof (3). The formulas not yet proved are (ii), (iii) and (vi), so the Challenge most likely means: Prove formulae (2), (3) and (6).

blocks.title: Recall!
blocks.text: \[\sqrt{x^{2}} = \begin{cases}x, & \text{if } x \ge 0 \\ -x, & \text{if } x < 0\end{cases}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A guide for the Challenge (the same method as the proofs above):
(ii) \(y = \cos^{-1} x\), \(y \in [0, \pi]\): \(\cos y = x\), so \(-\sin y\frac{dy}{dx} = 1\). On \([0, \pi]\), \(\sin y = \sqrt{1 - x^{2}} \ge 0\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\), \(x \in (-1, 1)\).
(iii) \(y = \tan^{-1} x\), \(y \in \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\): \(\tan y = x\), so \(\sec^{2} y\frac{dy}{dx} = 1\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{1 + \tan^{2} y} = \frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\).
(vi) \(y = \csc^{-1} x\), \(y \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] - \{0\}\): \(\csc y = x\), so \(-\csc y\cot y\frac{dy}{dx} = 1\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{1}{x\cot y}\). Here \(\cot y = \sqrt{x^{2} - 1}\) when \(x > 1\) and \(-\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}\) when \(x < -1\), so \(x\cot y = |x|\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}}\).

blocks.title: Example 6
steps:
Given: \(y = x\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) - \sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}}\) (with \(a > 0\) and \(|x| < a\), as the book's working assumes).
To find: \(\frac{dy}{dx}\).
Method: the first term is a product, so use the product rule, with formula (ii) and the chain rule for \(\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)\); the second term is a square root, so use the power rule with the chain rule.

Step 1: Differentiate w.r.t. x
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)\]
\[\quad + x\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (x/a)^{2}}} \cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)\right)\]
\[\quad - \dfrac{1}{2}(a^{2} - x^{2})^{-1/2} \cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}(a^{2} - x^{2})\]
Why: product rule on \(x \cdot \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)\) (the derivative of \(x\) is 1); \(\frac{d}{dx}\cos^{-1} u = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - u^{2}}}\frac{du}{dx}\) with \(u = \frac{x}{a}\); and \(\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}} = (a^{2} - x^{2})^{1/2}\).

Step 2: Work out the inner derivatives
\[= \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right) - \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{\frac{a^{2} - x^{2}}{a^{2}}}} \cdot \dfrac{1}{a}\]
\[\quad - \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}}}(-2x)\]
Why: \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) = \frac{1}{a}\), \(\frac{d}{dx}(a^{2} - x^{2}) = -2x\), and \(1 - \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} = \frac{a^{2} - x^{2}}{a^{2}}\).

Step 3: Simplify
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right) - \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}}}\]
\[\quad + \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}}}\]
\[= \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)\]
Why: \(\sqrt{\frac{a^{2} - x^{2}}{a^{2}}} = \frac{\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}}}{a}\) for \(a > 0\), so the second term is \(\frac{x \cdot a}{\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}}} \cdot \frac{1}{a} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}}}\); the last two terms cancel.
Check: take \(a = 2\), \(x = 1\). The answer gives \(\cos^{-1}\frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi}{3} \approx 1.0472\). Numerically, \(\frac{y(1.001) - y(0.999)}{0.002} \approx 1.0472\). They agree.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Example 6 uses \(\sqrt{a^{2}} = a\), so it takes \(a > 0\) (and \(|x| < a\) so that the square root is real). For \(a < 0\) we would have \(\sqrt{a^{2}} = -a\), and the two terms would no longer cancel.
Our examples:
(a) \(\frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}(2x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 4x^{2}}} \cdot 2 = \frac{2}{\sqrt{1 - 4x^{2}}}\), \(|x| < \frac{1}{2}\).
(b) \(\frac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}(x^{2}) = \frac{1}{1 + x^{4}} \cdot 2x = \frac{2x}{1 + x^{4}}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \((\sin^{-1} x)' = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\), \((\tan^{-1} x)' = \frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\), \((\sec^{-1} x)' = \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}}\); the co-functions have the same with a minus sign.
2. Proof method: write the inverse as a trigonometric equation, differentiate implicitly, change back to x.
3. The principal range decides the sign of every square root; this is why |x| appears in (v) and (vi).
4. With a chain: \(\frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1} u = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - u^{2}}}\frac{du}{dx}\), and similarly for the others.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Confusing \(\sin^{-1} x\) with \(\frac{1}{\sin x}\): the \(-1\) means inverse function, not reciprocal.
2. Writing \(\frac{1}{x\sqrt{x^{2} - 1}}\) for \((\sec^{-1} x)'\): without \(|x|\) the sign is wrong for \(x < -1\).
3. Forgetting the chain-rule factor, e.g. \(\frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}(2x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 4x^{2}}}\) (the factor 2 is missing).
4. Using the formulas at \(x = \pm 1\), where (i), (ii), (v), (vi) are not defined.
